title: Effective algorithms for finite generation of non-reductive invariant rings

problemStatement.formal: \text{Does there exist a uniform effective algorithm } \mathcal{A} \text{ such that, given an algebraic group } G \text{ acting linearly on } V = k^n, \, \mathcal{A} \text{ decides whether } k[V]^G \text{ is finitely generated as a } k\text{-algebra and (when finite) outputs a generating set?}
problemStatement.plain: Hilbert's 14th problem asks when the invariant ring k[V]^G is finitely generated. For reductive groups (finite, semisimple, tori, GL_n), the answer is yes and Derksen (1999) gave an explicit algorithm. For non-reductive groups, finite generation can fail (Nagata 1959: G_a^13 ⟶ k^32; Roberts 1990: 7-variable counterexample) but also holds in important cases (Weitzenboeck 1932: G_a in characteristic 0). The open question is whether there exists a uniform effective procedure that decides finite generation across non-reductive group actions and computes a generating set when one exists.
whyMatters: Sharpens Hilbert's 14th from an existence question to a computability question.
Connects classical invariant theory to modern computer algebra (Derksen's algorithm, Gröbner bases, locally nilpotent derivation kernels).
Foundational locally nilpotent derivation (LND) theory has no current Mathlib coverage; this slug provides a pedagogical anchor for formalizing the framework.
Adjacent to the Jacobian Conjecture (which is equivalent to a statement about G_a actions on polynomial rings).

proven: Derksen 1999: effective algorithm for k[V]^G when G is reductive (computes generators via the Hilbert nullcone).
Noether 1916: for finite G with char k not dividing |G|, generators of k[V]^G have degree at most |G| (giving an explicit enumeration-Reynolds-averaging algorithm).
Weitzenboeck 1932 (reproved Seshadri 1962): for G_a acting linearly on a polynomial ring over a field of characteristic zero, k[V]^{G_a} is finitely generated.
Zariski 1954: if the quotient variety has dimension at most 2, k[V]^G is finitely generated regardless of group reductivity.
Hochster-Roberts 1974: for reductive G, k[V]^G is Cohen-Macaulay (refined structure beyond mere finite generation).
open: Existence of a uniform effective algorithm across all algebraic group actions (the OQ-04 conjecture).
Decidability of finite generation for G_a^k actions when k is between 4 and 12 (Nagata's threshold is 13; Roberts' counterexample uses k=6 in 7 variables).
Sharp degree bound for invariant generators in the modular case (char k divides |G|), beyond Symonds 2011 partial bound.
knownResults.goal: Formalize Noether's degree bound (1916) as the algorithmic refinement of Hilbert's positive finiteness theorem for finite-group invariants, plus an Mathlib-tractable framework for locally nilpotent derivations sufficient to state Weitzenboeck's theorem and (axiom-form) Nagata's counterexample.

insights: OQ-04 is a meta-mathematical conjecture about algorithm existence; it cannot be formalized as a single Lean theorem. Lean progress must instead anchor on specific algorithmic refinements (Noether degree bound, slice theorem, etc.).
Noether's bound (deg ≤ |G|) is the highest-leverage S2 target: distinct from OQ-01's structural Reynolds infrastructure, provable from Mathlib primitives, foundational algorithmically.
OQ-01's `reynoldsSum` and `InvariantSubset` are directly reusable; the S2 OQ-04 file should cross-reference rather than redefine.
Mathlib has no locally nilpotent derivation framework. Weitzenboeck's theorem and the slice theorem are tier-2 axioms until `IsLocallyNilpotent` is defined.
Nagata's and Roberts' counterexamples are pedagogically essential but Lean-unprovable in any reasonable scope; they will live as axioms.
